description_full: Accenture plc provides consulting and managed services in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. It offers artificial intelligence and data; cloud consulting; cybersecurity consulting; digital engineering and manufacturing; ecosystem partners; emerging technology; finance and risk management consulting; infrastructure and capital projects; digital learning; supply chain consulting; technology consulting; sustainability consulting; and metaverse solutions, as well as customer services. The company also provides proprietary assets and platforms, such as GenWizard, SynOps and reinvention.AI to clients. It serves aerospace and defense, automotive, banking, capital markets, chemicals, communications and media, consumer goods and services, energy, health, high tech, industrial, insurance, life sciences, natural resources, private equity, public service, retail, software and platforms, travel, and utilities industries. Accenture plc was founded in 1951 and is based in Dublin, Ireland.
ceo_bio: Ms. Julie T. Spellman Sweet J.D. | CEO & Chairman | Age 58 | Compensation: $6.8M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 814K people. Revenue per employee of $91K ranks in the bottom quartile among Technology peers, with revenue growing 8%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $14K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $3K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 74× revenue per employee (elevated relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Accenture plc is a large-cap technology business with a $148.0B market cap on $74.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 36% against a 9% cost of capital — a 27-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $11.6B in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.48× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 38× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 7.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Insiders are net sellers (77% sell ratio) over the past year
Significant goodwill (36% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Technology sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 7% over 3 months
Elevated sector volatility (38% annualized) adds uncertainty
Antitrust and platform-regulation risk — the larger the network effect, the larger the regulatory target on its back, and a single consent decree can reset the moat.
AI disruption of existing software moats — incumbents with durable margins face commoditisation as AI-native competitors replicate features at a fraction of the R&D cost.
Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

Trading at a 49% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
Valued at a 34% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
20 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Technology peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 9pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.66x).
It accounts for 1.7% of sector revenue and 1.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-9.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 11% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 41% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 14% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 50% and a beta of 0.95, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.19 vs 5y 0.94), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.1B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 33% in the 2020 crash, 38% in the 2022 bear market and 35% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 49% below its DCF fair value of $492, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 42%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $370 to $666 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 18.5 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 11.2 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 12.7 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 25% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $233 on average, 7% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 36% clears the cost of capital of 9.0% by 27pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.98).
It converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.48x.
ROE of 27% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.4% of revenue on R&D and 2.8% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $2.7B (2% of market cap).
Goodwill makes up 36% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.0% over 3 years, 8.0% over 5 years and 7.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 13% of profits supports about 4.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.7% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.04, a backlog worth 50% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 8%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 1.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 21, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 86%.
Insider trading is two-way: 3 purchases and 10 sales over the past year, net $1.5M sold.
It returns 7.8% a year to shareholders (5.1% in buybacks and 2.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 20 consecutive years, raising it 9.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 814,000 employees, each generates about $91K of revenue, 0.2x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 7.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $14K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $6.8M (74x revenue per employee).
